title: What consistency model would you choose for this system, and why?
summary: The interviewer isn't testing whether you can define strong, eventual, and causal consistency — they're testing whether you can pick one per feature and defend the cost.

slides.markdown:
An interviewer asking "what consistency model would you use here?" is testing something narrower than it sounds: not whether you can define **strong**, **eventual**, and **causal** consistency, but whether you can pick the right one for a specific feature and defend the user-facing cost. Most candidates fail this by naming all three models correctly and never actually choosing one.

This topic gives you the skeleton for answering it live: pick per feature, state the cost of being wrong, and stay ready when the interviewer adds a curveball feature mid-answer.

Before naming a model, ask which specific operation the interviewer means. **"This system" almost never needs one consistency model** — a social app might need strong consistency for payments, eventual for a like counter, and causal for a comment thread, all in the same request path.

A good clarifying question: "are you asking about the write path for X, or how reads see it afterward?" This signals you already know consistency is chosen per data type, not per system, and buys you a second before committing.

If the interviewer insists on "just pick one for the whole system," push back briefly, then answer anyway — refusing to answer is worse than answering with a caveat.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: pick per feature, state the cost, commit
slides.markdown:
The skeleton that works under pressure: **name the feature, state the cost of being wrong in each direction, then commit.** For a bank balance, showing a stale number risks a user overdrawing — pick strong. For a view counter, showing a number 30 seconds behind costs nothing a user would notice — pick eventual.

Saying "it depends" and stopping there reads as evasive. Saying "it depends, and here's how I'd decide for this case" reads as senior. The interviewer isn't grading whether you land on the textbook-correct model — they're grading whether you have a repeatable method for choosing one.

Keep the skeleton to three moves: feature, cost of being wrong, decision.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: three features, three models
slides.markdown:
Applying the skeleton to three concrete features from a typical social-commerce app:

| Feature | Model | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Bank/wallet balance | Strong | A stale read can let a user spend money that isn't there — the cost of being wrong is real financial loss |
| Follower/view counter | Eventual | A count off by a few for a few seconds costs nothing a user notices or acts on |
| Comment thread ordering | Causal | A reply must never appear before the comment it replies to, but exact global order across unrelated threads doesn't matter |

The deciding question is never "how important is this feature" — it's "what does the user do with a stale value, and does that action cause harm."

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: implementing causal consistency for the comment thread
slides.markdown:
If the interviewer pushes further — "walk me through actually building the causal case" — implementing causal consistency for the comment thread means every reply carries a reference to the comment it replies to, and the read path enforces that a reply is never shown until its parent is visible on that replica.

Concretely: each write carries a **vector clock or parent-write timestamp**; a replica serving a reply checks it has already applied the parent write, and if not, delays serving the reply (or fetches the parent from a caught-up replica) rather than showing an orphaned reply.

This is weaker than strong consistency — unrelated threads can still be out of order across replicas — but strong enough that no user ever sees a broken conversation.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a fourth feature, named live
slides.markdown:
A common escalation: the interviewer says "now classify search-result ranking" with no warning. Don't panic-recite the three definitions — run your own skeleton out loud: "what does a user do with a stale ranking? Probably nothing they'd notice within a few seconds, and re-running the same query twice giving slightly different order is already normal for search. Eventual, with a short staleness window."

The interviewer is checking that your method generalizes, not that you memorized four answers in advance. Classifying it live, using the same feature-cost-decision shape you already established, is the actual signal they're looking for.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Say this unprompted: **stronger consistency costs latency and availability during a network partition; weaker consistency costs correctness the user can directly see.** Neither cost is free — naming which one this specific feature can least afford is the actual answer to "why."

| Choice | You pay in | You gain |
|---|---|---|
| Strong | Latency (cross-region round trips), availability during a partition | No stale reads, ever |
| Eventual | A window where reads can be stale | Low latency, keeps serving during a partition |
| Causal | Coordination cost between related writes only | Ordering guarantees only where they matter |

Naming this trade-off before the interviewer asks for it is what separates "knows the terms" from "can design with them."

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "instant AND always correct" — what do you tell product?
slides.markdown:
When product asks for "instant and always correct," the honest answer is that you can pick where on that line you sit, but you cannot erase the trade-off. Say so plainly, then reframe: "instant for the parts where staleness is invisible, correct-guaranteed for the parts where it isn't — let's go feature by feature."

This is also a chance to push back productively: ask which specific user complaint they're trying to prevent. Often "always correct" really means "never show a number that visibly moves backward," which is a much narrower and cheaper guarantee than global strong consistency.

A stakeholder-friendly framing for eventual consistency, with no CAP-theorem vocabulary: "when you do something, everyone sees it within a couple of seconds — not instantly, but fast enough nobody notices in normal use." Anchor it to a number they can picture (2 seconds, not "eventually") and a feature they already use elsewhere, like a like-count catching up a beat after they tap it.

Avoid the word "eventual" itself in the pitch — to a non-engineer it sounds like "maybe never." Naming the actual bound and a familiar comparison earns more trust than the term does.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: one consistency model for the whole system
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll just say strong consistency for the whole system — it's the safest answer."

**Why it's wrong:** applying strong consistency everywhere means every read pays a coordination cost even for data where staleness is harmless, capping scalability and latency for zero user-facing benefit. It also signals you haven't actually thought about the feature — you've picked the answer that sounds safest to say.

**Correct model:** consistency is chosen per feature based on the real cost of a stale read, never applied uniformly as a system-wide default.

"I pick consistency per feature, not per system — I ask what a user does with a stale value and whether that causes real harm. Strong where staleness causes damage (money, inventory), eventual where it's invisible (counters, view state), causal where relative order matters more than absolute freshness (comment threads, chat). Every choice trades latency and availability against visible staleness, and I name that trade-off explicitly rather than defaulting to whatever sounds safest."

See [consistency-models](consistency-models) for the underlying definitions this skeleton assumes you already know.
